# Codex rollout fixtures

These reduced fixtures target **Codex CLI 0.160.0** (`codex-cli 0.160.0`, checked locally). Most are synthetic; `vscode-context.jsonl` preserves the relevant metadata and usage values observed in a local 0.160.0 rollout, with message content, instructions and paths removed and timestamps simplified. It demonstrates that a valid session may use `source: "vscode"`; filtering to CLI/exec labels loses its context line. No fixture contains real conversations or credentials. Their envelope and field names were verified against the tagged upstream implementation:

- [Rollout serialization](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/history/src/rollout_payload.rs): `session_meta`, `turn_context`, `compacted`, `event_msg` with `payload`.
- [Protocol](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/protocol/src/protocol.rs): `SessionMeta`, `TurnContextItem`, `ThreadSettingsAppliedEvent`, `TokenUsageInfo`; `TokenUsage::tokens_in_context_window` uses `last_token_usage.total_tokens`, including output and reasoning already counted in the total. `total_token_usage` is cumulative; cached input is already included in input tokens.
- [Rollout recorder](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/rollout/src/recorder.rs): the writer keeps the current JSONL file open; new sessions create it lazily, resumed sessions open their existing file. Without the daemon this gives process-specific association without guessing from cwd, timestamps or the newest session.
- App-server daemon (observed locally with 0.160.0, not a tagged source): Codex installs `codex app-server --listen unix:// --managed-daemon` under `CODEX_HOME/packages/app-server-daemon/` and writes its pid to `CODEX_HOME/app-server-daemon/daemon.pid` (`{"pid":…}`). The TUI talks to it over `app-server-control/app-server-control.sock`; the daemon holds every rollout open (labelled `source: "vscode"`) and keeps a finished one open about 60 seconds. Nothing on disk links a TUI's pid to its thread, so cornercase then falls back to the folder: one open rollout of the daemon with the agent's cwd, written since the agent was first seen, and one Codex TUI in that folder.
- [Rollout names](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/rollout/src/rollout_file_name.rs): `rollout-<timestamp>-<thread-id>[_<rollout-id>].jsonl`.
- [Thread settings](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/core/src/session/thread_settings.rs): model changes persist `thread_settings_applied`, including the owning thread ID.
- [npm wrapper](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-cli/bin/codex.js): Node spawns the native binary with inherited stdio and environment, then waits for it.

cornercase shows the rounded share used, `last_token_usage.total_tokens / model_context_window`, capped at 100%. It does not reproduce Codex's remaining-percentage adjustment for a 12,000-token baseline, infer a window from the model, or add cached/reasoning tokens a second time.

The reader follows only Codex children of the foreground process, selects one open rollout with a CLI, exec or VSCode source under that process's `CODEX_HOME/sessions` (or `HOME/.codex/sessions`), and checks the header's ID against its filename. Association depends on the owning process; the source label alone does not identify which session is in a pane. Subagent rollouts and ambiguous matches are omitted. Linux uses `/proc`; macOS uses `proc_listchildpids` and `/usr/sbin/lsof -n -P -a -p <pid> -Fn`. macOS needs its system `lsof` and permission to inspect the same user's process. Unavailable process metadata or a remote/container session yields no line. The fake-agent tests run on Linux and macOS in CI without contacting any model.

Fixtures cover current versus lifetime usage, cached/reasoning accounting, model changes, compaction and missing/malformed data. Additional generated cases test incremental writes, invalid windows, truncation, replacement, deletion, concurrent sessions, wrapper children, configured homes and process exit.

`reply.jsonl` keeps the shape of the `response_item` lines a local 0.160.0 rollout wrote for a turn, with the text replaced: the user's message, an assistant `message` with `phase: "commentary"` (a progress note), a tool call, the assistant `message` with `phase: "final_answer"` and the `task_complete` event, whose `last_agent_message` repeats it. Assistant text is `output_text` items in `content`; `read --last-message` takes the newest such message, whatever its phase, and the line's `timestamp`.

`turn-started.jsonl`, `turn-complete.jsonl` and `turn-aborted.jsonl` keep the shape of the `task_started`, `task_complete` and `turn_aborted` events a local 0.160.0 rollout wrote for a turn that finished and one interrupted with Esc, with ids, times and the reply replaced. cornercase counts a pane as working between a start and the next completion or abort. Approval requests are not written to the rollout; they show only in Codex's terminal title (`[ ! ] Action Required` and `[ . ] Action Required`, alternating), which `src/activity.rs` reads.

`user-message.jsonl` keeps the shape of the two lines a local 0.160.0 rollout wrote when Codex took a prompt (0.161.0 writes the same): a `response_item` user message whose `content_item_kinds` is `user.text` (the instructions and environment Codex adds are user messages too, with other kinds) and an `item_completed` event whose item is a `UserMessage`, with ids, text and times replaced. `cornercase send --enter` confirms a prompt from that event's `timestamp`. A prompt sent while a turn runs is held in Codex's memory (`Messages to be submitted after next tool call`) and written only when Codex takes it, after its next tool call or when the turn ends (checked live on 0.161.0).
